This page gives the intuition behind every function in the package, with no
code. Each section ends with a pointer to the article that shows it in
practice.

## The question

You measured the same features (genomic positions, days, proteins...) in
two or more experimental groups, with several replicates per group. You want
to know, feature by feature or as a whole, **how different the groups are**,
with an honest account of the uncertainty that few replicates leave.

## Data: one row per observation

Every analysis starts from a long table with five columns: `ID` (the
feature), `Group`, `Sample` (the replicate), `Input` (a numeric position for
the feature) and `Output` (the measurement). `Input` is what gives the
features a geometry: two features with close `Input` values are expected to
behave alike.
See [Basic pipeline](01_basic_pipeline.html) and
[Real data](03_real_data.html).

## The kernel: encoding "close features behave alike"

A **kernel** is a function `k(x, x')` returning how strongly two features at
positions `x` and `x'` co-vary. A Squared Exponential kernel says the
correlation decays smoothly with distance, at a rate set by its
*length scale*; adding a *noise* term accounts for measurement noise, and a
*variance* term sets the overall amplitude. These few numbers are the
**hyperparameters**, and they are learned from the data by maximum
likelihood (`fit_kernel()`), not chosen by hand.
See [Kernel choice](08_kernel_choice.html).

## The posterior: what we believe about each group

With the kernel fixed, each group gets a **posterior distribution** over
its vector of feature values: a mean (the smoothed, replicate-averaged
profile) and a covariance (how uncertain each feature is, and how
uncertainties are tied together). Fewer replicates give a wider posterior;
a shared kernel means groups are described by the same notion of closeness.
`posterior_mean()` computes this in closed form.
See [Pooled vs. non-pooled](04_pooled_vs_nonpooled.html) and
[Unequal sample sizes](07_unequal_sample_size.html).

## Comparing groups: a distance between posteriors

Comparing two groups means comparing two Gaussian posteriors. Two summaries
cover most needs:

- the **overlapping coefficient (OVL)**: the share of probability mass the
  two posteriors have in common, from 0 (disjoint) to 1 (identical);
- the **Wasserstein distance**, a distance in the units of the data, which
  we normalise per feature so that it does not grow with the number of
  features.

OVL is intuitive but saturates near 0 once many features are compared
jointly; the normalised Wasserstein stays readable. `group_diff()` picks
between them for you from the number of features.
See [Choosing a metric](06_metric_choice.html) and
[More than two groups](05_multi_group.html).

## Scale: when there are many features

The posterior involves a covariance matrix as large as the number of
features, and inverting it becomes costly. **Block-diagonal** fitting
splits the features into independent blocks, trading a little cross-block
correlation for a much smaller problem per block.
See [Block-diagonal partition](10_block_diagonal.html) and
[Performance at a glance](11_performance.html).

## Assumptions to keep in mind

- Within a group, each feature sits at one `Input` position (or one
  position per dimension), and every group being compared shares the same
  set of features.
- Replicates of a feature within a group are exchangeable: the model has no
  built-in notion of pairing or batch.
- Posteriors are Gaussian: the model targets continuous, roughly symmetric
  measurements (transform counts or proportions first when needed).

## Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ID` | Identifier of a feature (position, protein, day...) |
| `Input` | Numeric location of a feature; drives the kernel |
| `Input_ID` | Index of the dimension when `Input` has several |
| Kernel | Function giving the covariance of two features from their positions |
| Hyperparameters | Kernel parameters (variance, length scale, noise) fitted from the data |
| Posterior | Distribution of a group's feature vector given the data |
| `pooled` | `TRUE`: one kernel for all groups; `FALSE`: one per group |
| OVL | Overlapping coefficient between two posteriors, in `[0, 1]` |
| Wasserstein | Distance between two posteriors, in the data's units |
| Block | Subset of features fitted independently of the others |
